a: harm will not lay hold of you
p: The Greek uses one word for the evil you do and the harm that comes back.
b: The Greek repeats kakos: do not do kaka (evil things), and kakon (evil, harm) will not seize you. English needs two words, "evil" and "harm," but the Greek ties them together: what you send out is what comes back. The Hebrew of MS A has the same repetition (2v:6-7): אל תעש לך רעה ואל ישיגך רעה, "Do no evil yourself and evil will not overtake you" (Parker and Abegg). This chapter begins a long run of short commands that start "Do not" (Greek mē), the style of a teacher drilling his students.
orig: καὶ οὐ μή σε καταλάβῃ κακόν (kai ou mē se katalabē kakon), "and evil will never seize you"

a: My son
p: Ben Sira speaks as a teacher to a pupil, the way Proverbs does.
b: Here the Greek has huie, "son"; at 10:28 and 11:10 it has teknon, "child," which this site renders "my child." Both stand for the Hebrew beni, "my son," the form of address of a teacher to his pupil, as in Proverbs 1:8 and Proverbs 6:1. MS A has beni at 10:28 (4r:13), 11:8 (4r:25) and 11:10 (4r:27-28), but not here (2v:7). Ben Sira taught young men in Jerusalem (51:23 calls his school a "house of instruction"), so "son" is a pupil as much as a child. The address includes daughters only by later application; the advice on wives and daughters in 7:19-26 and chapter 9 shows the pupils were men.
orig: υἱέ (huie), "son"

a: the furrows of injustice
p: The farmer's image of sowing and reaping wrong is old in Israel's wisdom and prophets.
b: Proverbs says it plainly: "Plant wrongdoing and you will harvest disaster" (Proverbs 22:8). Hosea accuses Israel: "You plowed wickedness. / You harvested injustice" (Hosea 10:13), and Job's friend Eliphaz had seen that those who plow trouble reap it (Job 4:8). Paul uses the same picture for the life of the Spirit: "Whatever a person sows, that is what he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). "Seven times over" means in full measure, as in Genesis 4:15 and Proverbs 6:31.
r: Proverbs 22:8; Hosea 10:13; Job 4:8; Galatians 6:7; Genesis 4:15; Proverbs 6:31

a: the power to lead
p: Ben Sira warns his pupils, who were trained for public life, against hunting for power.
b: Scribes in Ben Sira's Jerusalem served rulers and sat in councils (8:8; 39:4), so the temptation to seek office was real for his students. The warning is not that office is evil but that a person may not be strong enough for it (7:6). The Greek hēgemonia is leadership or command; MS A has memshelet, "rule" (2v:8). Compare Jesus' warning not to grab the place of honor at a feast (Luke 14:8-11).
orig: ἡγεμονίαν (hēgemonian), "leadership, command"

a: Do not claim to be in the right before the Lord
t: No one is in the right before God
p: Ben Sira agrees with Job, the Psalms and Paul that no one can stand on his own record before God.
b: The Greek verb dikaioō, "declare righteous, justify," here in the middle voice, means "do not justify yourself." The thought matches the 66 books: "how can a mortal be in the right with God?" (Job 9:2), and the psalmist's plea, "no living person is in the right in your presence" (Psalm 143:2). Jesus told of a Pharisee who listed his virtues and a tax collector who only begged for mercy, and said the second went home justified (Luke 18:9-14). Ben Sira draws no doctrine of justification from it; his point is humility.
orig: μὴ δικαιοῦ ἔναντι Κυρίου (mē dikaiou enanti Kyriou), "do not justify yourself before the Lord"

a: a stumbling block
t: A trap for your own honesty
p: A judge who fears the powerful trips up his own integrity.
b: The Greek skandalon is the trigger of a trap, then anything that makes a person fall; it is the word the New Testament uses for a stumbling block or snare (Matthew 18:7; Romans 14:13). A judge who is afraid of a powerful man will bend his ruling, and so he sets a trap in the path of his own "uprightness" (euthytēs, straightness). The Law forbids a judge to favor the great (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:17). MS A ends the line differently (2v:11): "and receive for it an undeserved blot on your integrity" (Parker and Abegg).
orig: θήσεις σκάνδαλον (thēseis skandalon), "you will set a stumbling block"

a: tie up a sin twice
p: The Greek says "do not bind a sin twice."
b: The verb katadesmeuō means to bind fast, and dis means "twice": "do not bind a sin twice." It may mean do not repeat a sin, or do not add a second sin to the first, for even the first one brings guilt. MS A (2v:12) uses the verb qashar, "tie," which can also mean "conspire": Parker and Abegg translate it "Do not conspire to repeat a sin." Someone later wrote this verse again in the margin of Codex Vaticanus at 12:12, as Swete's notes show.
orig: μὴ καταδεσμεύσῃς δὶς ἁμαρτίαν (mē katadesmeusēs dis hamartian), "do not bind a sin twice"

a: He will notice how many gifts I bring
p: Ben Sira shares the prophets' warning that offerings do not cover a wrong life.
b: The man Ben Sira quotes thinks the size of his offerings will make God overlook his sins. The 66 books say the same as Ben Sira: "When the wicked sacrifice, the LORD finds it abhorrent" (Proverbs 15:8), and Isaiah has God refuse a multitude of sacrifices from hands full of blood (Isaiah 1:11-15). Ben Sira returns to this later, on the offerings of the unjust (31:21-27 in the Greek order, 34:18-22 in the KJV) and the sacrifice of keeping the law (32:1-26 Greek, chapter 35 KJV). He is not against sacrifice: in 7:29-31 he tells his pupils to give the priests their full share. MS A has no line for this verse; see the variant.

a: God Most High
p: Ben Sira often calls God "the Most High," a title as old as Genesis.
b: The Greek hypsistos, "highest," stands for the Hebrew Elyon. Melchizedek blesses Abram by "God Most High" (Genesis 14:19), and the title is common in the Psalms. Ben Sira uses it often (7:15; 9:15; 12:2, 6). The Greek of Sirach has no divine name: Kyrios is "the Lord," never "the LORD," because the translator, like all Greek translators, put Kyrios where the Hebrew had the name.
orig: θεῷ ὑψίστῳ (theō hypsistō), "to God Most High"

a: giving alms
p: The Greek says "alms"; the Hebrew says tsedaqah, "righteousness," the later Jewish word for charity.
b: The Greek eleēmosynē, from eleos, "mercy," means a gift to the poor. MS A (2v:14) has ובצדקה אל תתעבר, "and in tsedaqah do not be wanting." In the Bible tsedaqah is "righteousness," but in Ben Sira and later Hebrew it also means charity, giving to the poor, as it still does in Jewish life. Ben Sira pairs prayer with almsgiving, as Tobit does (Tobit 12:8) and as Jesus does in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:1-6).
orig: ἐλεημοσύνην (eleēmosynēn), "alms, mercy shown to the poor"

a: there is One who brings low and lifts high
t: The God who brings low and lifts up
p: Hannah's song and Mary's song both praise the God who reverses people's fortunes.
b: Hannah sang, "he puts them down, and he also raises them up" (1 Samuel 2:7), and Mary sang, "He has pulled rulers down from thrones / and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52). Ben Sira draws a practical lesson: since God can turn things around, do not mock a person in bitter trouble, for tomorrow you may be the one laid low. The theme returns in 10:14-15 and 11:5-6, 12-13.

a: plow up a lie
p: The Greek plows a lie; MS A plows violence.
b: The Greek arotriaō means "to plow"; MS A (2v:16) has tacharosh, "plow, devise," with "violence" (chamas) as its object where the Greek has "a lie." In Hebrew the verb charash means both to plow and to plot (Proverbs 3:29; Proverbs 6:14), and the Greek translator kept the farmer's image instead of turning it into plain "devise," as the KJV does. It follows the sowing of 7:3.
orig: μὴ ἀροτρία ψεῦδος (mē arotria pseudos), "do not plow a lie"

a: do not say the same words over and over when you pray
p: Jesus gives a similar warning about prayer in the Sermon on the Mount.
b: The Greek deuteroō means to do a second time, to repeat. Jesus said, "When you are praying, do not chatter on like the Gentiles. They imagine that all their talking will get them a hearing" (Matthew 6:7). Ecclesiastes advises, "let your words be few" before God (Ecclesiastes 5:2). Ben Sira links talk in prayer with talk in the council of elders: in both places, babbling is a lack of respect. This is a warning against empty words, not against praying often (Luke 18:1).
orig: μὴ δευτερώσῃς λόγον (mē deuterōsēs logon), "do not repeat a word"

a: farm work, which the Most High created
p: Ben Sira says farm work was created by God, a view rooted in Genesis.
b: In Genesis, God put the man in the garden "to work it and to guard it" (Genesis 2:15) before the curse made the work painful (Genesis 3:17-19). Ben Sira, a scribe who prized study (38:24-34), still tells his pupils not to look down on hard physical work. MS A puts this line earlier, right after 7:8 (2v:13-14), and says the work "has been apportioned to you by God" (Parker and Abegg).

a: fire and the worm
t: Fire and worm: punishment after death?
p: The Greek speaks of fire and the worm for the ungodly; MS A speaks only of worms for every mortal.
b: The Greek line echoes Isaiah 66:24, "their worm will not die, / and their fire will not be put out," which Jesus quotes for Gehenna: "where their worm never dies and the fire is never put out" (Mark 9:48). Judith 16:17 also has "fire and worms" for God's enemies. MS A reads differently (2v:19-20): כי תקות אנוש רמה, "for the hope of a mortal is worms": all humans end in the grave, so be humble. The Greek reads "the punishment of the ungodly"; see the variant on this verse. Elsewhere Ben Sira says that no one in Hades praises the Most High (17:27) and that in Hades no one asks how long a life was (41:4), so he does not build a doctrine of punishment after death on this line.

a: the gold of Ophir
p: Ophir was the land of the finest gold; the Greek spells it Souphir.
b: The Greek has Soupheir. The Greek Old Testament spells the place in several ways (Sōphēra in 1 Kings 9:28, Sōpheira in 2 Chronicles 8:18). Ophir was the far-off land (perhaps in Arabia, Africa or India) where Solomon's ships fetched gold (1 Kings 9:28; 1 Kings 10:11). "Gold of Ophir" was proverbial for the best gold (Job 22:24; Job 28:16; Psalm 45:9). MS A (2v:21) has בזהב אופיר, "for the gold of Ophir." A true friend is worth more than the best gold, as a good wife is in the next verse.
orig: χρυσίῳ Σουφείρ (chrysiō Soupheir), "gold of Souphir"

a: something that does not matter
p: The Greek says "for something indifferent"; the Hebrew says "for a price."
b: The Greek adiaphoros means something that makes no difference, of no account. MS A (2v:21) reads bimchir, "for a price": do not sell a friend for money. Either way the point is the worth of a friend, a theme Ben Sira treats at length in chapter 6 (6:5-17) and again in 9:10 and 12:8-9.
orig: ἕνεκεν ἀδιαφόρου (heneken adiaphorou), "for the sake of something indifferent"

a: a wise and good wife
p: Ben Sira echoes Proverbs: a good wife is a treasure beyond price.
b: Proverbs says, "The one who finds a wife has found something good, / and he draws favor from the LORD" (Proverbs 18:22), and asks, "A woman of strength, who can find one? / Her price is far beyond red coral" (Proverbs 31:10). MS A (2v:22) says her charm is worth more than peninim, the same precious stones (or corals) of Proverbs 31:10; the Greek says "gold," picking up the gold of the verse before. Ben Sira returns to wives in 9:1-2, chapters 25-26 and 36:23-31 (Greek numbering).
orig: γυναικὸς σοφῆς καὶ ἀγαθῆς (gynaikos sophēs kai agathēs), "a wise and good woman (wife)"

a: do not hold back his freedom
p: The "servant" here is a household slave, and Ben Sira urges giving him his freedom.
b: The Greek oiketēs is a household servant, usually a slave, and eleutheria is freedom, release from slavery. The Law of Moses set a Hebrew slave free in the seventh year: "In the seventh he goes free, owing nothing" (Exodus 21:2; compare Deuteronomy 15:12-15). Jeremiah condemned the rich of Jerusalem who freed their slaves and then took them back (Jeremiah 34:8-17). MS A (2v:23-24) reads "Cherish a prudent servant as your own soul" (Parker and Abegg). Ben Sira assumes slavery, as his whole world did; here he urges kindness and release. At 30:33-40 (Greek numbering; 33:24-31 in the KJV) he gives harsher advice about slaves.
orig: μὴ στερήσῃς αὐτὸν ἐλευθερίας (mē sterēsēs auton eleutherias), "do not deprive him of freedom"

a: Look after them
p: Ben Sira follows Proverbs' practical advice on caring for animals.
b: Proverbs says, "Make sure you know the faces of your sheep; / set your heart on your herds" (Proverbs 27:23). The Greek episkeptou means "look after, watch over," the same verb used for visiting the sick in 7:35. Verses 22-26 run through a household: animals, sons, daughters, wife, the way the household codes of the New Testament later run through wives, children and slaves (Colossians 3:18-4:1).
orig: ἐπισκέπτου αὐτά (episkeptou auta), "look after them"

a: Discipline them
p: Paideuō covers teaching and correcting; here, with "bend their necks," it means discipline.
b: The verb paideuō (noun paideia) means to bring up a child: to train, teach and correct. This site renders paideia "discipline" where correction is in view and "instruction" where the sense is teaching. Here "bend their necks" shows that correction is meant, so the Plain English Translation says "Discipline them," as Proverbs speaks of the father who "seeks him out early with discipline" (Proverbs 13:24). Where the sense is teaching, this part has "instruction" (8:8) and "instruct" (10:1), and the person without schooling is "untaught" (8:4; 10:3). MS A uses the verb yasar, "discipline," in the first line (2v:25) but has a different second line: "and take wives for them in their youth." See the variant on this verse.
orig: παίδευσον αὐτά (paideuson auta), "discipline them, train them"

a: do not turn a beaming face toward them
p: The Greek idiom means not to be too easy on a daughter.
b: Literally "do not make your face cheerful toward them." MS A (2v:26-27) reads ואל תאיר אלהם פנים, "do not make your face shine on them," the language of favor (Numbers 6:25). Ben Sira wants a father to be strict and watchful with his daughters, because a daughter's honor, and her family's, depended on her chastity before marriage (Deuteronomy 22:13-21). He comes back to a father's worry over daughters in 42:9-14, a passage the Talmud quotes (Sanhedrin 100b). This is the advice of a man of his time; the Plain English Translation does not soften it.
orig: μὴ ἱλαρώσῃς πρὸς αὐτὰς τὸ πρόσωπόν σου (mē hilarōsēs pros autas to prosōpon sou)

a: Do not drive her out
p: To "drive out" a wife meant to divorce her.
b: The Greek ekballō, "throw out," is the language of divorce: a husband sent his wife out of his house (Deuteronomy 24:1). Ben Sira tells a man who has a wife he loves not to divorce her. Malachi says the LORD hates divorce (Malachi 2:16), and Jesus forbade it (Mark 10:2-12). The first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, MS A and the Latin add a line about a wife who is hated; see the variant.
orig: μὴ ἐκβάλῃς αὐτήν (mē ekbalēs autēn), "do not throw her out"

a: Honor your father with all your heart
p: Ben Sira restates the commandment and gives a reason: remember your mother's labor.
b: The command is the fifth (in Catholic and Lutheran counting the fourth) of the Ten Commandments: "Honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12). Ben Sira has already taught on it at length in 3:1-16. Here he adds the reason of gratitude: they gave you life, and you can never pay them back (7:28). The Catholic Catechism quotes 7:27-28 for this very point (see the chapter page). MS A has no line for 7:27-28: it goes straight from 7:26 to 7:29 (2v:28).

a: with all your soul
p: Verses 29-30 echo Deuteronomy 6:5, "with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength."
b: The great commandment says, "Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:5). The Greek of 7:29-30 says "with all your soul" and "with all your strength" (dynamis, the word of the Greek Deuteronomy 6:5). MS A has "with all your heart" (2v:28) and "with all your might," בכל מאודך (bekhol me'odekha, 3r:1), the exact word of Deuteronomy 6:5. Ben Sira takes the love owed to God and applies it to the honor owed to his priests. Jesus called this the first commandment (Mark 12:29-30).

a: Give him his share
p: Ben Sira lists the portions the Law gives the priests.
b: The Greek list follows the Law: the "guilt offering" (Leviticus 5:14-6:7; Leviticus 7:1-7), whose meat went to the priests; "the gift of the shoulders," the foreleg the priest received from every sacrifice (Deuteronomy 18:3, "the foreleg," Greek brachiona, the word used here); "the sacrifice of consecration," probably the offerings that set things apart as holy; and the first fruits (Numbers 18:12-13). Priests had no land of their own and lived on these gifts (Numbers 18:20). MS A lists other gifts: "the meat of bulls," heave offerings and "sacrifices of righteousness" (3r:2-3, Parker and Abegg, with some letters uncertain); see the variant. Ben Sira admired the priests, above all the high priest Simon (chapter 50).
orig: δόσιν βραχιόνων (dosin brachionōn), "a gift of shoulders (forelegs)"

a: so your blessing will be made whole
p: Giving to the poor completes a person's religion after the offerings to the priest.
b: The Greek teleioō means to complete, to make perfect. After the gifts to the priests (7:31), Ben Sira says your blessing is not complete until you also open your hand to the poor. Deuteronomy commands: "Open your hand wide to your brother, to the poor and the needy among you in your land" (Deuteronomy 15:11). MS A (3r:4) reads tishlam, "may be complete."
orig: ἵνα τελειωθῇ ἡ εὐλογία σου (hina teleiōthē hē eulogia sou)

a: do not keep your kindness from the dead
p: What kindness is owed the dead? Burial and mourning at least; some read more into it.
b: The Greek charis is grace, favor, kindness; MS A (3r:5) has chesed, "loyal love": וגם ממת אל תמנע חסד. Naomi blessed the LORD, "who has not abandoned his faithful love for the living and the dead" (Ruth 2:20). The plainest reading is the duty to bury the dead and to mourn them, which Tobit risks his life to do (Tobit 1:17-18; Tobit 2:3-8), and the next verse turns to mourning. The first line differs in MS A: "Give generously to all the living" (Parker and Abegg).
orig: ἐπὶ νεκρῷ μὴ ἀποκωλύσῃς χάριν (epi nekrō mē apokōlysēs charin)

a: grieve along with those who grieve
p: Paul gives almost the same command in Romans.
b: Paul writes, "Be glad along with the glad. Weep along with those who weep" (Romans 12:15). The Greek of both passages joins the verb to "with" (meta here, meta in Romans 12:15 too). In Jewish practice, comforting mourners became one of the great works of kindness, beside visiting the sick (the next verse) and burying the dead (7:33).

a: visit the sick
p: Jesus counts visiting the sick as service done to him.
b: The Greek episkeptesthai means to look in on, to visit with care. Jesus says, "When I was sick, you took care of me" (Matthew 25:36), using the same verb, and James calls true religion "to visit orphans and widows in their trouble" (James 1:27). Later Jewish teaching counts visiting the sick (bikkur cholim) among the deeds of loving-kindness. MS A has a different line, with nothing about the sick (3r:6): "Do not withdraw your heart from your friend" (Parker and Abegg); see the variant.
orig: ἐπισκέπτεσθαι ἄρρωστον (episkeptesthai arrōston), "to visit a sick person"

a: remember your last end
p: The Greek ta eschata, "the last things," became the Latin "memorare novissima tua."
b: The Greek ta eschata sou means "your last things," the end of your life. MS A (3r:6-7) has acharit, "end, outcome": בכל מעשיך זכור אחרית, "in all your deeds remember the end," and its second line, where the Greek has "you will never sin," reads "you will not see corruption for all eternity" (Parker and Abegg). The psalmist prays to be taught to number his days (Psalm 90:12). In the Latin Vulgate this verse is 7:40: "memorare novissima tua," "remember your last things." Ben Sira means death; Christian readers later heard in "the last things" death, judgment, heaven and hell.
orig: μιμνήσκου τὰ ἔσχατά σου (mimnēskou ta eschata sou), "remember your last things"

a: gold has ruined many people
p: Ben Sira warns that money corrupts, as the Law and Paul do.
b: The Law forbids bribes, "for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise" (Deuteronomy 16:19; compare Exodus 23:8). Paul warns that those who want to get rich fall into a trap, and that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil (1 Timothy 6:9-10). Ben Sira's point is practical as well as moral: a poor man cannot win a fight with a rich one, because money buys judges and even kings. In MS A (3r:10) gold "has broken the restraint of many" (Parker and Abegg); the end of the line is partly lost.
orig: πολλοὺς γὰρ ἀπώλεσεν τὸ χρυσίον (pollous gar apōlesen to chrysion), "for gold has destroyed many"

a: do not pile wood on his fire
p: Proverbs uses the same picture for a quarrel kept alive by talk.
b: Proverbs says, "When the wood runs out, the fire dies, / and when there is no gossip, the fighting calms down" (Proverbs 26:20), and the next verse compares a quarrelsome man to charcoal on embers (Proverbs 26:21). The "man who talks too much" (Greek glōssōdēs, "all tongue") is the person whose quarrel grows with every word you answer. James calls the tongue a fire (James 3:5-6).
orig: ἀνθρώπου γλωσσώδους (anthrōpou glōssōdous), "a tongue-ful man"

a: every one of us is liable to be punished
p: Ben Sira grounds mercy toward the repentant in the guilt everyone shares.
b: The Greek en epitimiois means "under penalties," liable to punishment; MS A (3r:13) says זכר כי כלנו חייבים, "remember that all of us are guilty." This matches the 66 books: "For there is no human being on the earth so righteous that he does good and does not sin" (Ecclesiastes 7:20), and Paul, "For all sinned, and all lack the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Paul draws the same practical lesson as Ben Sira: restore a fallen brother gently, "Look to yourself, in case you are tempted as well" (Galatians 6:1). Jesus' story of the lost son condemns the brother who will not welcome a sinner home (Luke 15:25-32).
orig: πάντες ἐσμὲν ἐν ἐπιτίμοις (pantes esmen en epitimois)

a: Do not slight a man when he is old
p: The Law commands respect for the aged, and Ben Sira gives the reason: we are all heading there.
b: Leviticus says, "Rise up before gray hair, and honor the face of the old" (Leviticus 19:32). Ben Sira adds a reason that anyone can feel: "there are those among us who are aging too." MS A (3r:13-14), with some letters uncertain, gives the reason as "we are all appointed to old age" (Parker and Abegg).

a: Do not gloat over anyone who has died
p: Proverbs forbids rejoicing when an enemy falls; Ben Sira extends it to death itself.
b: Proverbs says, "When your enemy falls, do not be glad, / and when he trips, keep your heart from cheering" (Proverbs 24:17). Ben Sira's reason is the fate everyone shares: "we all come to our end." MS A (3r:14) says זכר כלנו נאספים, "remember: all of us are gathered in," the old phrase for dying and joining one's ancestors (Genesis 25:8). The KJV's "thy greatest enemy" comes from a longer Greek text; see the variant.

a: their proverbs
p: The Greek "proverbs" stands for a Hebrew word that also means riddles.
b: The Greek paroimiai, "proverbs, sayings," is the word the Greek Proverbs uses for its own title. MS A (3r:15) has ובחידתיהם התרטש: "their riddles" (chidot), the word of Proverbs 1:6, with a rare verb that Parker and Abegg translate "carefully analyze." A scribe learned by memorizing and puzzling over the sayings of earlier teachers, as Ben Sira says in 39:1-3.
orig: ἐν ταῖς παροιμίαις αὐτῶν ἀναστρέφου (en tais paroimiais autōn anastrephou)

a: how to serve important men
p: Ben Sira's students were trained to serve rulers, so this is career advice.
b: The Greek leitourgēsai megistasin means "to serve great men," to be of use in the courts of the powerful. In Ben Sira's day Judea was ruled by Greek kings, first the Ptolemies of Egypt and then the Seleucids of Syria, after Antiochus the Great took Judea (Josephus, Antiquities 12.129-133), with a high priest and a council of elders in Jerusalem. Educated scribes served as advisers, envoys and record-keepers. In 39:4 Ben Sira says the scribe will serve among great men and appear before rulers.
orig: λειτουργῆσαι μεγιστᾶσιν (leitourgēsai megistasin)

a: for they in turn were taught by their fathers
p: Wisdom passes from father to son, from teacher to student.
b: Moses says, "Ask your father, and he will tell you, / your old ones, and they will explain" (Deuteronomy 32:7), and Bildad tells Job to learn from the former generation (Job 8:8-10). Ben Sira's chain of learning, the old learning from their fathers and teaching the young, is the same idea that later Jewish tradition put at the head of the Mishnah's tractate Avot: the Torah handed down from Moses through a line of teachers. Ben Sira himself is a link in such a chain.

a: give ground to an insolent man
p: The Greek is unclear: do not leave your place, or do not rise up in anger?
b: The Greek exanastēs apo prosōpou means "rise up from before the face of." It may mean "do not get up and leave" (give way to him), or "do not rise up against him"; the Greek allows both. The KJV reads "Rise not up in anger." The Plain English Translation takes the first sense, the one MS A has (3r:19): אל תזוח מפני לץ, "Do not fall back before a mocker" (Parker and Abegg). If you give ground, he will sit in your place and wait to catch you out in your words. The Greek hybristēs is the man of hybris, "insolence" (10:6).
orig: μὴ ἐξαναστῇς ἀπὸ προσώπου ὑβριστοῦ (mē exanastēs apo prosōpou hybristou)

a: Do not stand good for more than you can manage
p: Ben Sira takes up Proverbs' warnings about guaranteeing loans, but is more willing to allow it.
b: To "stand good for" a person is to guarantee his debt (Greek engyaō; Hebrew 'arav). Proverbs warns hard against it: "My son, if you have stood good for your neighbor, / if you have struck palms for an outsider," get yourself free at once (Proverbs 6:1-5; compare Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 22:26-27). Ben Sira softens the rule: do it only within your means, and expect to pay. In 29:14-20 he praises the good man who stands good for his neighbor and warns of the ruin it can bring.
orig: μὴ ἐγγυήσῃ ὑπὲρ δύναμίν σου (mē engyēsē hyper dynamin sou)

a: Do not take a judge to court
p: A judge's colleagues will side with him because of his rank.
b: The Greek says "they will judge for him according to his glory (rank, reputation)." In a world without independent courts, a lawsuit against a judge would be heard by his friends. MS A (3r:21-22) says he will decide "as he pleases," with the verb partly lost. The Law demands that judges not show favor (Deuteronomy 16:18-20), but Ben Sira describes how things often were.
orig: κατὰ γὰρ τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ κρινοῦσιν αὐτῷ (kata gar tēn doxan autou krinousin autō)

a: Do not pick a fight with a hot-tempered man
p: Proverbs gives the same warning about hot-tempered company.
b: Proverbs says, "Do not keep company with a man ruled by anger, / and do not go along with someone full of rage" (Proverbs 22:24), for you may learn his ways. Ben Sira adds the danger of the open road: in the desert, where there is no one to help, a man who thinks nothing of blood may kill you. Travel through the Judean wilderness was dangerous, as the story of the man who fell among robbers on the road to Jericho shows (Luke 10:30).

a: he will not be able to keep a word quiet
t: A fool cannot keep a secret
p: Proverbs contrasts the gossip with the faithful friend who keeps a matter covered.
b: The Greek logon stexai means "to keep a word covered," to keep a confidence. Proverbs says, "One who goes around telling tales lays bare what was said in confidence, / but one with a faithful spirit keeps the matter under cover" (Proverbs 11:13). MS A uses poteh, the naive or simple person of Proverbs (3r:25-26): כי לא יוכל לכסות סודך, "for he cannot cover your secret."
orig: λόγον στέξαι (logon stexai)

a: you cannot know what it will give birth to
p: Ben Sira borrows Proverbs' picture of time "giving birth" to the unknown.
b: Proverbs says, "Don't brag about tomorrow, / since you cannot know what a day will give birth to" (Proverbs 27:1). Ben Sira uses the same verb (Greek tiktō, "give birth"; Hebrew of MS A yeled, 3r:26) for a secret told before a stranger: you cannot know what it will lead to. The Talmud quotes a Ben Sira saying with the same phrase, "you do not know what a day will bring" (Yevamot 63b).

a: pay you back with a favor
p: The Greek is hard; MS A has a different line: do not drive good things away from yourself.
b: The Greek mē anapheretō soi charin means "let him not bring back a favor to you." The verb anapherō means "bring back," and also "carry off." The sense is unclear. It may be that a person you confide in repays your trust with a show of kindness that hides harm, as the Latin takes it ("lest he bring false favor on you," 8:22 there) and the KJV ("lest he requite thee with a shrewd turn"); or that he carries off your good standing. MS A has a different line (3r:27): "lest you drive good things from yourself" (Parker and Abegg); see the variant. The Plain English Translation translates the Greek.
orig: καὶ μὴ ἀναφερέτω σοι χάριν (kai mē anapheretō soi charin)

a: Do not be jealous over the wife you hold close
p: Ben Sira warns that suspicion can teach a wife the very thing feared.
b: The "wife of your bosom" (Greek gynaika tou kolpou sou) is the beloved wife, as in Deuteronomy 13:6 and Micah 7:5. The Law had a ritual for a jealous husband who suspected his wife (Numbers 5:11-31). Ben Sira gives practical advice instead: constant jealousy teaches "an evil lesson" that turns against the husband, either by giving his wife the idea, or by teaching her to deceive. The Greek says "teach against yourself" (epi seauton); MS A has "lest you teach yourself an evil lesson" (3r:28, Parker and Abegg). Chapter 9 is written to young men about women; it says nothing to women about men, and reflects the society Ben Sira taught in.
orig: Μὴ ζήλου γυναῖκα τοῦ κόλπου σου (mē zēlou gynaika tou kolpou sou)

a: she tramples on your strength
p: The Hebrew says "to make her tread on your high places," a picture of conquest.
b: The Greek epibēnai autēn epi tēn ischyn sou means "for her to step upon your strength," to master you. MS A (3v:1) reads להדריכה על במותיך, "to make her tread on your high places," the picture of a conqueror standing on the heights of a defeated land, as in Deuteronomy 33:29: "you will tread on their high places." Proverbs' Lemuel is told, "Do not hand your strength over to women" (Proverbs 31:3).
orig: ἐπιβῆναι αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τὴν ἰσχύν σου (epibēnai autēn epi tēn ischyn sou)

a: a woman who sells her company
p: The Greek names a Greek kind of paid companion; the Hebrew has Proverbs' "strange woman."
b: The Greek hetairizomenē comes from hetaira, "companion," the word for the educated courtesans of Greek cities, women paid for company and sex. MS A (3v:1) has אל תקרב אל אשה זרה, "do not go near a strange woman," the figure of Proverbs: "Honey drips from the strange woman's lips" (Proverbs 5:3); "to guard you from the strange woman" (Proverbs 7:5). So MS A has the Hebrew figure of Proverbs, and the Greek has the word for a Greek courtesan.
orig: γυναικὶ ἑταιριζομένῃ (gynaiki hetairizomenē)

a: a woman who plays the harp
p: Women musicians at banquets were often also hired for sex.
b: The Greek psallousa is a woman who plays a stringed instrument; a later hand in Codex Vaticanus wrote above it lyrizousēs, "playing the lyre," as Swete's notes show. At Greek drinking parties such women were hired to entertain, and often to do more. Isaiah mocks Tyre as a forgotten prostitute who takes up her harp and walks the city (Isaiah 23:15-16). MS A (3v:3) warns against lying down with "a musician" and her "devious words" (Parker and Abegg).
orig: μετὰ ψαλλούσης μὴ ἐνδελέχιζε (meta psallousēs mē endelechize)

a: pay the penalty for her
p: The Law made a man who seduced an unmarried girl pay her bride-price.
b: The Greek epitimia are penalties or fines. The Law says, "If a man lures away a virgin who is not promised in marriage and lies with her, he must pay her bride-price and take her as his wife" (Exodus 22:16; see Deuteronomy 22:28-29, fifty shekels of silver). MS A (3v:4), פן תוקש בעונשיה, "lest you be snared by her fines," says the same. Job had "cut a covenant with my eyes" not to look at a young girl (Job 31:1), and Jesus taught that a lustful look is already adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28).
orig: ἐν τοῖς ἐπιτιμίοις αὐτῆς (en tois epitimiois autēs), "in her penalties"

a: you will lose what you inherited
p: Proverbs warns that a man who keeps company with prostitutes wastes his wealth.
b: Proverbs says that a man who keeps company with prostitutes wastes his wealth (Proverbs 29:3). Jesus' story of the lost son has him squander his share, and his brother charges that he spent it on prostitutes (Luke 15:13, 30). The "inheritance" may be the family land, which an Israelite was meant to keep in the family for good (Numbers 36:7-9).

a: Keep your eye off a woman with a lovely figure
p: Ben Sira and Proverbs both locate the start of adultery in the eye.
b: Proverbs warns, "Do not crave her beauty in your heart; / do not let her catch you with her eyelids" (Proverbs 6:25). David's sin began when he saw a beautiful woman bathing (2 Samuel 11:2). MS A (3v:6) begins העלים עין מאשת חן, "Hide your eye from a shapely woman" (Parker and Abegg). The Talmud quotes the Hebrew of 9:8-9. In the William Davidson translation of Sanhedrin 100b on Sefaria it reads: "Avert your eyes from a woman of grace, lest you be trapped in her snare. Turn not to her husband to mix wine and strong drink with him, as many have been corrupted by the beauty of the beautiful woman, and mighty are all her fatalities." Yevamot 63b quotes the same lines in a slightly different form. In Sanhedrin 100b Rav Yosef names them among the good passages of Ben Sira that may be taught even in public.

a: another man's wife
t: A married woman, or her husband?
p: The Greek says "a married woman"; the same Hebrew letters in MS A can be read "her husband."
b: The Greek hypandros means "under a husband," a married woman. MS A (3v:7) has עם בעלה אל תטעם. Written without vowels, the letters b-'-l-h can be read be'ulah, "a married woman" (the word of Isaiah 62:4, "Married"), as the Greek took them and as Parker and Abegg translate ("another man's wife"), or ba'lah, "her husband," as the Talmud quotes the line: "Do not turn to her husband to mix wine and strong drink with him" (Yevamot 63b, William Davidson translation). Either way the warning is against the drinking party that leads to adultery.
orig: μετὰ ὑπάνδρου γυναικὸς (meta hypandrou gynaikos)

a: slide down to ruin
t: Sliding to ruin, or to bloodshed
p: The Hebrew adds blood: the angry husband may kill you.
b: The Greek says "in your spirit you may slip into destruction." MS A (3v:8) reads ובדמים תטה אל שחת, "and in blood you slide down to the Pit." The "blood" may be the death penalty for adultery (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22) or the revenge of a jealous husband, which Proverbs describes: "Jealousy is the fury of a man, / and on the day of revenge he will not hold back" (Proverbs 6:34). See the variant.
orig: ὀλισθήσῃς εἰς ἀπώλειαν (olisthēsēs eis apōleian), "you slip into destruction"

a: New friend, new wine
p: Jesus uses the same comparison of old and new wine.
b: Ben Sira compares a new friend to new wine: it needs time to age before it is good. Jesus said, "Besides, no one who has been drinking the old wants the new. 'The old is good,' he says" (Luke 5:39). Proverbs also prizes the old friend: "Your friend and your father's friend, do not abandon them" (Proverbs 27:10). MS A ends, "But it is when it is old that you will drink it" (3v:10, Parker and Abegg, with part of the verb restored).

a: Do not envy a sinner's glory
p: Ben Sira repeats a frequent warning of the Psalms and Proverbs.
b: "Do not burn up inside over people who do evil; / do not envy those who do wrong" (Psalm 37:1). "Do not let your heart be jealous of sinners; / be jealous instead for the fear of the LORD, all day long" (Proverbs 23:17). Psalm 73 tells of a man who nearly fell because he envied the wicked, until he saw their end (Psalm 73:3, 17). The Greek katastrophē, "overthrow," gives us the word "catastrophe."
orig: ἡ καταστροφὴ αὐτοῦ (hē katastrophē autou), "his overthrow"

a: right up to Hades they will not be acquitted
p: Hades is the Greek word for Sheol, the world of the dead.
b: The Greek hadēs, the god and the world of the dead in Greek religion, was used by the Greek translators for Hebrew she'ol, the place where all the dead go. MS A (3v:11) has no word for the world of the dead here: זכר כי עת מות לא ינקה, "Remember that at the time of death he will not go unpunished" (Parker and Abegg). The point in both is that the wicked do not escape: they are punished by the time they die, the view of retribution in this life that runs through the book (11:26). It is not a statement about judgment after death.
orig: ἕως ᾅδου οὐ μὴ δικαιωθῶσιν (heōs hadou ou mē dikaiōthōsin)

a: a man who has power to kill
p: Ben Sira knew the danger of life near a king who could execute at will.
b: In a Hellenistic court, the king or his governor held the power of life and death. Proverbs says, "A king's fury is death's messengers" (Proverbs 16:14). Ben Sira's pupils, who might serve such men (8:8), are told to keep their distance, and if they must come near, to make no mistakes. "Walking along the top of city walls," the battlements, is a picture of a place where one wrong step means a fall.

a: the law of the Most High
t: The law of the Most High
p: For Ben Sira, wisdom and the Law of Moses go together.
b: The Greek nomos is "the law," for Ben Sira the Law of Moses. Talk among the wise should be "about the law of the Most High." This joining of wisdom and Torah is one of the book's great themes: in 24:23 Wisdom is identified with "the book of the covenant of God Most High," and in 39:1 the scribe gives himself to the study of the law. Psalm 1 blesses the one who murmurs God's law day and night (Psalm 1:2). Compare the saying of Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion in Mishnah Avot 3:2: when two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Shekhinah, the Presence of God, rests among them.
orig: ἐν νόμῳ Ὑψίστου (en nomō Hypsistou)

a: let the fear of the Lord be what you boast in
t: Boasting in the fear of the Lord
p: Jeremiah says the only right boast is in knowing the LORD.
b: The Greek kauchēma is a boast, a ground of pride. Jeremiah says, "If anyone is to boast, let it be in this alone: / that he shows insight and knows me" (Jeremiah 9:24), and Paul applies it: "Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:31). The phrase "the fear of the Lord" (Greek phobos Kyriou) is Proverbs' great theme (Proverbs 1:7), and it returns in Ben Sira again and again, as in 10:19-24.
orig: ἐν φόβῳ Κυρίου ἔστω τὸ καύχημά σου (en phobō Kyriou estō to kauchēma sou)

a: A loudmouth is feared in his city
p: Proverbs and James warn of the reckless tongue.
b: The Greek anēr glōssōdēs, "a tongue-ful man," is the same word as in 8:3. Proverbs says the one who opens his lips wide comes to ruin (Proverbs 13:3), and James calls the tongue "a small member" that can set a whole forest on fire (James 3:5). MS A (3v:17-18) ends, "one who takes matters up upon his mouth is hated" (Parker and Abegg).
orig: ἀνὴρ γλωσσώδης (anēr glōssōdēs)

a: Like the people's judge, so are his officials
p: Proverbs makes the same observation about rulers and their servants.
b: Proverbs says, "When a ruler pays attention to false words, / every one of his servants turns wicked" (Proverbs 29:12). The officials (Greek leitourgoi, "those who serve," the word used for the priests' helpers in 7:30) take their tone from the man at the top. In MS A this verse and the next are in the other order (3v:19-20).
orig: οἱ λειτουργοὶ αὐτοῦ (hoi leitourgoi autou), "his officials"

a: Authority over the earth is in the Lord's hand
p: Daniel and Paul say the same: rulers hold power by God's appointment.
b: Daniel praises God: "he removes kings and he sets kings up" (Daniel 2:21; compare Daniel 4:17). Paul writes, "There is no authority that does not come from God" (Romans 13:1), and Proverbs says, "the king's heart lies in the LORD's hand" (Proverbs 21:1). The Greek exousia, "authority," is Paul's word in Romans 13:1. For Ben Sira this is comfort and warning at once: God raises up the right leader "at the right time," and he can take him away (10:8, 14).
orig: ἐν χειρὶ Κυρίου ἐξουσία τῆς γῆς (en cheiri Kyriou exousia tēs gēs)

a: the scribe
p: A scribe was a trained expert in writing and in the law; Ben Sira was one.
b: The Greek grammateus is a scribe: a man trained to read and write, to keep records and to teach the law. Ezra "was a scribe, an expert in Moses' law" (Ezra 7:6), and Ben Sira describes the scribe's calling in 38:24-39:11. The line in MS A that matches this one (3v:21) has mechoqeq, "lawgiver, ruler": ולפני מחוקק ישית הודו, "and before the lawgiver he sets his majesty." MS A puts this verse before 10:4. The Greek reads "the scribe."
orig: προσώπῳ γραμματέως (prosōpō grammateōs), "the face of a scribe"

a: Do not hold a grudge against your neighbor
p: The Law forbids keeping a grudge; MS A forbids paying evil back to a neighbor.
b: The Greek mēniaō means to nurse anger, to keep a grudge. Leviticus says, "Do not take vengeance, and do not keep a grudge against the children of your people. You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). MS A (3v:22-23) reads "for every offense do not repay evil to a neighbor" (אל תשלים רע לריע, with the first letter of the line restored), close to Paul's rule: "Pay no one back evil for evil" (Romans 12:17).
orig: μὴ μηνιάσῃς τῷ πλησίον (mē mēniasēs tō plēsion)

a: Kingdoms are carried from one nation to another
p: Ben Sira lived through one empire handing Judea over to another.
b: The Greek basileia ... metagetai means "kingship is moved." Daniel speaks of kingdoms rising and falling (Daniel 2:21, 37-45). In Ben Sira's world a kingdom had changed hands: in the reign of Antiochus the Great, the Seleucid king of Syria took Judea from the Ptolemies of Egypt, and the Jews received him into Jerusalem (Josephus, Antiquities 12.129-133). Ben Sira's reasons are moral: wrongdoing, insolence and money bring empires down. MS A (3v:25) has "on account of violence and pride" (Parker and Abegg).
orig: βασιλεία ἀπὸ ἔθνους εἰς ἔθνος μετάγεται (basileia apo ethnous eis ethnos metagetai)

a: dust and ashes
p: The phrase is Abraham's, and the Greek is the same as in the Greek Genesis.
b: Abraham says, "I am only dust and ashes" (Genesis 18:27); the Greek there, gē kai spodos, is the same as here, and MS A (3v:25-26), מה יגאה עפר ואפר, "why is dust and ashes proud?", matches Genesis' 'afar va'efer. Job uses it too (Job 30:19; Job 42:6). Humans come from dust and return to it (Genesis 3:19), so pride is absurd.
orig: γῆ καὶ σποδός (gē kai spodos), "earth and ashes"

a: I have thrown his insides away
p: A hard line: the Greek of Vaticanus says "I threw away," as if God were speaking.
b: Codex Vaticanus, as Swete prints it, reads errhipsa, "I threw away," and Swete's notes give no other reading for the first hand of Sinaiticus, for Alexandrinus or for Ephraemi. Read that way, the speaker breaks into the poem: even while a proud man lives, "I" have flung out his bowels, perhaps meaning that disease rots the living body. Minuscules 157 and 248 read "they threw away" (Fritzsche), and the Latin projecit, "he has cast away," takes it of the miser who throws away his own life (see the variant). MS A (3v:26) reads אשר בחייו יורם גויו, which Parker and Abegg translate "that it should lift up its heart during its life": a verb of rising, not of throwing. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.
orig: ὅτι ἐν ζωῇ ἔρριψα τὰ ἐνδόσθια αὐτοῦ (hoti en zōē errhipsa ta endosthia autou)

a: the doctor jokes
t: The doctor jokes, or cuts it off?
p: Vaticanus says the doctor "jokes" at a long illness; two later copies say he "cuts it off."
b: The Greek of Vaticanus is skōptei, "mocks, jests." It may mean the doctor makes light of a long illness, or that a lingering sickness makes a fool of the doctor, and the king who is well today is dead tomorrow. Minuscules 157 and 248 read koptei, "cuts off" (Fritzsche), and the KJV follows that reading: "The physician cutteth off a long disease." MS A (3v:26-27) reads differently again: שמץ מחלה יצהיב רופא, "'The smallest illness,' laments the physician" (Parker and Abegg). See the variant. Ben Sira honors physicians in 38:1-15.
orig: σκώπτει ἰατρός (skōptei iatros), "the doctor jests"

a: creeping things, wild animals and worms
p: Isaiah says the same of the proud king of Babylon.
b: Isaiah mocks the fallen king: "Under you, maggots make your mattress; / worms are your bedcovers" (Isaiah 14:11). Job says of the rich and the poor in the grave, "Both lie down in the same dust, / and the maggot spreads over them" (Job 21:26). MS A (3v:28) lists four kinds of creatures: "maggots and worms, flies and creeping things" (Parker and Abegg). The word "inherit" is bitter irony: a man works all his life to leave an inheritance, and what he himself inherits is worms.

a: Human pride begins when a man turns away from the Lord
p: Ben Sira defines pride by its root: leaving the God who made you.
b: The Greek aphistamenou apo Kyriou uses the verb from which "apostasy" comes. For Ben Sira, pride is not only thinking too much of oneself; it is the heart pulling away from its Maker. Proverbs says, "Pride comes before a crash, / a lofty spirit before a stumble" (Proverbs 16:18), and Genesis tells the first sin as a grab at being like God (Genesis 3:5). This agrees with the 66 books. Thomas Aquinas, who read the line in the Latin (10:14 there, "apostatare a Deo"), quoted it as an objection to calling pride the beginning of every sin, and answered that turning away from God here means the general condition of every sin (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 84, article 2, objection and reply 2).
orig: ἀνθρώπου ἀφισταμένου ἀπὸ Κυρίου (anthrōpou aphistamenou apo Kyriou)

a: sin is where pride begins
p: Vaticanus says sin is the beginning of pride; other witnesses and the Latin say pride is the beginning of sin.
b: Swete's text (Vaticanus) reads archē hyperēphanias hamartia, "the beginning of pride is sin." The first hand of Codex Alexandrinus and minuscule 248 have it the other way round, "the beginning of sin is pride," and so does the Latin, initium omnis peccati est superbia, "pride is the beginning of all sin" (10:15 in the Vulgate; see the variant). In that form Augustine cites it in The City of God (14.13): "For pride is the beginning of sin" (in Marcus Dods's translation). Thomas Aquinas puts it in the "On the contrary" of his article "Whether pride is the beginning of every sin" (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 84, article 2), and explains that pride is first in what a sinner aims at, while greed (1 Timothy 6:10) is the root in the means. MS A (4r:1) reads כי מקוה זדון חטא, "the reservoir of presumption is sin" (Parker and Abegg), closer to Vaticanus.

a: pulled down
p: Mary's Magnificat says almost the same words.
b: Mary sings, "He has pulled rulers down from thrones / and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52). The Greek of Luke, katheilen dynastas apo thronōn kai hypsōsen tapeinous, uses the same verb as here, katheilen, "pulled down," with "thrones" and the lifting up of the lowly. Luke's song is full of the language of the Greek Old Testament (1 Samuel 2:7-8; Job 12:19), and Ben Sira shows that this hope of God reversing the proud and the humble was alive among Jews in the centuries before Jesus. Whether Luke knew Sirach itself cannot be shown. MS A and the Latin name the proud here; see the variant.
orig: θρόνους ἀρχόντων καθεῖλεν ὁ κύριος (thronous archontōn katheilen ho kyrios)

a: planted the humble in their place
p: The image moves from thrones to roots: God uproots nations and plants the lowly.
b: The Greek tapeinous is "humble, lowly," the same root as "humble yourself" in 7:17. God as a gardener who uproots and plants is the picture of Jeremiah's call, "to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant" (Jeremiah 1:10). Verses 14-17 form a little hymn on what the Lord has done to proud nations. MS A has no line that matches this verse: it goes from 10:14 to the line that matches 10:16 (4r:3).
orig: ἐφύτευσεν ταπεινοὺς ἀντ᾽ αὐτῶν (ephyteusen tapeinous ant' autōn)

a: children born of women
p: An old Hebrew phrase for frail human beings.
b: Job says, "A human, born of a woman, / is short of days and has his fill of turmoil" (Job 14:1), and Jesus says, "no one born of a woman has ever been raised up who is greater than John the Baptist" (Matthew 11:11). Ben Sira's point: pride and fierce anger do not fit creatures so weak. MS A (4r:6) uses the same phrase, לילוד אשה (lilud ishshah).

a: What race is honored? The human race.
p: Ben Sira asks the same question twice and gives two answers each time.
b: The Greek sperma is "seed," offspring, a race or line. The riddle runs: which line is honored? Humanity, made in God's image; but within it, those who fear the Lord. Which line is despised? Humanity, since it sins; but within it, those who break the commandments. Honor comes from fear of God, not from birth. The KJV follows a longer Greek text with different words (see the variant). MS A has a shorter form of the riddle (4r:6-7).
orig: σπέρμα ἔντιμον ποῖον; σπέρμα ἀνθρώπου (sperma entimon poion? sperma anthrōpou)

a: the first step to being accepted
t: A line mended by an editor
p: This bracketed line survives only in two later copies, damaged; the sense "accepted" is Fritzsche's correction.
b: The great codices have no verse 21, and neither MS A nor the Latin has this line. It stands after 10:20 in two later Greek copies, minuscules 106 and 248, but in a damaged form: 106 begins prolēpseōs and 248 pro lēxeōs. Fritzsche wrote proslēpseōs, "acceptance," in their place, saying so in his notes ("ego scripsi," "I have written"), and the Plain English Translation translates his wording. So "accepted" and "thrown out" give the sense as Fritzsche mended it. See the variant for what each copy has.
orig: προσλήψεως ἀρχή (proslēpseōs archē), "the beginning of acceptance," Fritzsche's correction

a: The rich, the honored and the poor
t: Rich, honored and poor; or sojourner and foreigner?
p: MS A lists the sojourner, a word read "scoundrel" or "insolent," the foreigner and the poor.
b: The Greek names three kinds of people, rich, honored and poor. MS A (4r:8) reads גר וזד נכרי ורש, which Parker and Abegg translate "Sojourner and scoundrel, foreigner and poor man": their glory is the fear of God (part of the word "fear" restored). The second word, zed, usually means an arrogant or insolent person. Kahana's 1912 edition prints zar, "stranger," which differs by one letter (resh for dalet). See the variant on this verse.
orig: πλούσιος καὶ ἔνδοξος καὶ πτωχός (plousios kai endoxos kai ptōchos)

a: a poor man who has understanding
p: James and Ecclesiastes protest the same contempt for the poor.
b: Ecclesiastes tells of a poor wise man who saved a city, yet no one remembered him: "a poor man's wisdom is looked down on, and no one listens to his words" (Ecclesiastes 9:16). James condemns a church that seats the rich man in the good place and tells the poor man to stand (James 2:1-6). Ben Sira says honor should follow understanding and the fear of the Lord, not wealth.

a: Free men will wait on a wise servant
p: Proverbs and the story of Joseph both show a wise slave rising above the free.
b: Proverbs says, "A servant with good sense will take charge of a son who brings disgrace, / and will get a share of the inheritance along with the brothers" (Proverbs 17:2). Joseph was sold as a slave and ended as ruler over Egypt (Genesis 41:39-43). MS A (4r:10) reads "A prudent servant is to be exalted" (Parker and Abegg). The KJV adds "when he is reformed," from the longer Greek; see the variant.

a: one who acts important and has no bread
p: Ben Sira retells a saying of Proverbs.
b: Proverbs says, "Better a man little thought of who has a servant / than one who acts important and has no bread" (Proverbs 12:9). Ben Sira takes the second line and adds a picture of the idle man who "wanders around." MS A (4r:12) is close to Proverbs in shape: "Better is one who works and has abundant wealth than one who honors himself but is lacking in means" (Parker and Abegg, with several letters restored). The Greek of Codex Sinaiticus adds "and has plenty," which the KJV follows ("aboundeth in all things").

a: My child
p: Teknon, "child," is the grandson's Greek for the teacher's "my son."
b: This is the first teknon, "child," in this part of the book. MS A (4r:13) has בני בענוה כבד נפשך, "my son, in humility honor your soul." The Plain English Translation renders teknon as "my child" each time (10:28; 11:10). See the note on "My son" at 7:3.
orig: τέκνον (teknon), "child"

a: bring honor to your soul by gentleness
p: Ben Sira asks for humility without self-contempt.
b: Right after his long warning against pride (10:6-18), Ben Sira says a person should still honor his own soul and give it "the respect it is due" (Greek kata tēn axian autēs, "according to its worth"). The way to do it is gentleness (praütēs, the "meekness" of Matthew 5:5). The next verse explains: the one who really dishonors himself is the sinner (10:29). Jesus joins love of neighbor to love of self, "love your neighbor as yourself" (Matthew 22:39).
orig: ἐν πρᾳύτητι δόξασον τὴν ψυχήν σου (en praütēti doxason tēn psychēn sou)

a: seats him among the great
t: The lowly wise man raised up
p: Joseph and Daniel are the Bible's great examples of wisdom lifting a lowly man to sit among rulers.
b: Proverbs says of the skilled worker, "He will take his place before kings, / not before people of no account" (Proverbs 22:29). Joseph rose from prison to rule Egypt because God gave him wisdom (Genesis 41:39-41), and Daniel, an exile, was set over the wise men of Babylon (Daniel 2:48). MS A (4r:18) uses dal, "poor," for the lowly man, and "nobles" (nedivim) for the great.
orig: σοφία ταπεινοῦ ἀνύψωσεν κεφαλήν (sophia tapeinou anypsōsen kephalēn)

a: Do not praise a man for his good looks
p: God told Samuel the same when he was choosing a king.
b: When Samuel was impressed by Eliab's height, the LORD said, "A human sees what is before the eyes, but the LORD sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Ben Sira applies it both ways: do not praise the handsome or despise the plain. MS A (4r:19) has a fuller second line: do not abhor a person who is "ugly in his appearance" (Parker and Abegg; the word "ugly" partly restored).

a: The bee is small
p: The Greek Proverbs also praises the bee, small but honored for its wisdom.
b: MS A (4r:20) says אליל בעוף דברה, "the bee is a nothing among birds," using 'elil, the word the prophets use for worthless idols. Ancient people counted the bee among flying creatures. The Greek of Proverbs has an addition after the ant (Proverbs 6:8 in Swete's text) that sends the reader to the bee as well, ending "though she is weak in strength, because she honors wisdom she is advanced": kaiper ousa tē rhōmē asthenēs, tēn sophian timēsasa proēchthē. Ben Sira draws the lesson for 11:1-2: do not judge worth by size or looks. Samson's riddle came from honey found in a lion (Judges 14:8).

a: what he does among people is hidden
p: Here MS A writes the divine name, as three yods.
b: The Greek says the works of Kyrios, "the Lord," are wonderful and hidden. MS A (4r:21) reads כי פלאות מעשי ייי, "for wonderful are the works of the LORD," writing the name YHWH as three yods, as it does elsewhere in these chapters (4v:4; 5r:2). Ecclesiastes says no one can know the work of God who makes everything (Ecclesiastes 11:5). The first half of the verse is different in MS A: "To the one who has only a loincloth do not feel superior and do not scoff at the bitterness of his day" (4r:20-21, Parker and Abegg).
orig: κρυπτὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀνθρώποις (krypta ta erga autou en anthrōpois)

a: Many absolute rulers have sat down on the ground
p: Greek tyrannoi are sole rulers, not necessarily cruel ones; the Hebrew turns the picture around.
b: The Greek tyrannoi means rulers who hold power alone, not "tyrants" in the English sense of cruel rulers; this site renders the word "absolute rulers," as in the Wisdom of Solomon. To "sit on the ground" is to mourn or to be humbled (Job 2:13; Isaiah 47:1). MS A (4r:22) says the reverse: רבים נדכאים ישבו על כסא, "many who were crushed have sat on a throne." Both lines say God reverses fortunes, as with Joseph and David, and the king of Ecclesiastes who "came out of the prison house to reign" (Ecclesiastes 4:14).
orig: πολλοὶ τύραννοι ἐκάθισαν ἐπὶ ἐδάφους (polloi tyrannoi ekathisan epi edaphous)

a: Give no answer until you have heard
p: Ben Sira retells Proverbs 18:13.
b: Proverbs says, "Giving a reply before you have heard / is foolish of you and a disgrace" (Proverbs 18:13). The Greek of both verses has prin akousai, "before hearing." Nicodemus used the same principle in defense of Jesus: "Our law does not judge a person unless it first hears from him and finds out what he is doing, does it?" (John 7:51). MS A (4r:25) begins with "My son."
orig: πρὶν ἢ ἀκοῦσαι μὴ ἀποκρίνου (prin ē akousai mē apokrinou)

a: a matter that is none of your business
p: Proverbs has a vivid picture of meddling in someone else's fight.
b: Proverbs says, "Someone who seizes a dog by the ears: / that is a passerby who gets angry over a fight that is not his" (Proverbs 26:17). MS A (4r:26) reads, "When there is nothing to irritate you, do not get angry" (Parker and Abegg). The second line forbids sitting with sinners when they judge, perhaps a warning against joining an unjust court (Psalm 1:1; Exodus 23:2).

a: do not take on too many affairs
p: Ben Sira warns against a life spread too thin.
b: The Greek praxeis are dealings, business. A person with too many affairs will not "stay free of blame" (Greek athōōthēsē, "be held innocent"), because some deal will go wrong. Jesus said to Martha, "you are worried and in a turmoil over many things" (Luke 10:41). MS A (4r:27) reads, "My son, why should you increase your troubles?" and warns that the one who hurries to multiply wealth "will not go unpunished" (Parker and Abegg), close to Proverbs 28:20.
orig: μὴ περὶ πολλὰ ἔστωσαν αἱ πράξεις σου (mē peri polla estōsan hai praxeis sou)

a: the Lord's eyes have looked on him for his good
t: God lifts the slow and the weak
p: Success is not only the reward of effort; God gives it as he wills.
b: Verses 11-13 set two men side by side: one hurries and falls behind, the other is slow and poor, yet God raises him. Ecclesiastes says, "the race does not belong to the swift... For time and chance meet them all" (Ecclesiastes 9:11), and Hannah sang, "He lifts the poor up out of the dust" (1 Samuel 2:8). Ben Sira does not say laziness is good; he says the outcome is in the Lord's hand (11:14).

a: Good and bad, life and death
t: Good and bad from the Lord
p: Ben Sira says both good and bad come from God, as Isaiah, Job and Lamentations do.
b: The 66 books say the same: "I make peace and create disaster. / I am the LORD, the maker of all these" (Isaiah 45:7); "Should we take the good from God, and not take the bad too?" (Job 2:10); "Do not troubles and good both go out from the mouth of the Most High?" (Lamentations 3:38). The "bad" here is misfortune, poverty and death, not sin: Ben Sira later says plainly that God does not make anyone sin (15:11-20), as James does (James 1:13). The longer Greek and the Latin add two more lines here; see 11:15-16.
orig: πτωχεία καὶ πλοῦτος παρὰ Κυρίου ἐστίν (ptōcheia kai ploutos para Kyriou estin)
r: Isaiah 45:7; Job 2:10; Lamentations 3:38; Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6-7; 15:11-20; James 1:13

a: The Lord's gift stays with the godly
p: The gift lasts for the godly: the Greek, the Latin and MS A agree.
b: The Greek eusebesin means "the godly, the devout." The Latin has justis, "the just," and MS A (4v:6) has tsaddiq, "the righteous." Swete's notes show only one other Greek reading, eulabesin, "the reverent," in a corrector of Sinaiticus. All of them say the same thing: the Lord's gift lasts for those who belong to him.
orig: παραμένει εὐσεβέσιν (paramenei eusebesin), "remains with the godly"

a: I have found rest
p: Jesus' parable of the rich fool tells the same story.
b: In Luke 12:16-21 a rich man plans bigger barns and says, "Soul, you have lots of good things stored up, enough for many years. Rest now. Eat, drink, celebrate" (Luke 12:19). God answers, "Fool! On this very night they demand your soul back from you. And what you have made ready, who will get it?" (Luke 12:20). Ben Sira's man says "I have found rest (anapausis), and now I will eat," and he too leaves his goods to others and dies. Jesus adds what Ben Sira only implies: such a man "is not rich toward God" (Luke 12:21). The likeness is close; whether Jesus or Luke knew Sirach cannot be proved, since the theme is common (Psalm 49:10; Ecclesiastes 2:18).
orig: Εὗρον ἀνάπαυσιν (heuron anapausin), "I have found rest"

a: Stand firm in your covenant
p: The Greek says "your covenant"; the Hebrew line in MS A is damaged.
b: The Greek diathēkē is the usual word for "covenant." Here it seems to mean the duty God has assigned you, your place in life, since the line goes on, "and grow old at your work." MS A is damaged at this line (4v:10); Parker and Abegg read it "continue in your trade and find security in it." The covenant of Israel with God may also be in view (17:12; 24:23).
orig: στῆθι ἐν διαθήκῃ σου (stēthi en diathēkē sou)

a: Trust the Lord and keep at your work
p: Psalm 37 gives the same advice to the person troubled by the success of the wicked.
b: "Go quiet before the LORD and wait for him with longing. / Do not burn up inside over someone whose way goes well" (Psalm 37:7). MS A has a vivid line (4v:11): "run to the LORD and hope for his light" (Parker and Abegg; some letters restored). The Greek pisteue tō Kyriō, "trust the Lord," is the verb of faith in the New Testament.
orig: πίστευε τῷ κυρίῳ (pisteue tō kyriō)

a: The Lord's blessing is the wage of the godly
p: Ben Sira takes up Proverbs' saying on the Lord's blessing.
b: Proverbs says, "It is the LORD's blessing that makes a person rich, / and toil adds nothing to it" (Proverbs 10:22). Ben Sira joins blessing to work: the godly keep at their toil (11:20-21), and God's blessing is their wage and can "bloom" (Greek anathallei, "make to sprout again") in a moment.

a: I have all I need
p: The self-satisfied rich man appears in the Law, the prophets and Revelation.
b: The Greek autarkē moi estin means "I am self-sufficient." Moses warned that when Israel grew rich it would forget the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:12-14), and Hosea says, "Full, they let their hearts swell with pride. / So they forgot me" (Hosea 13:6). The risen Christ says to the church in Laodicea, "You say, 'I am rich. I have grown wealthy, and I need nothing.'" (Revelation 3:17).
orig: Αὐτάρκη μοί ἐστιν (autarkē moi estin)

a: On a good day the bad is forgotten
p: Ecclesiastes gives similar advice about good and bad days.
b: "On a good day, enjoy the good, / and on a bad day, take a look: / God made this one to match that one" (Ecclesiastes 7:14). Ben Sira observes that each kind of day blots out memory of the other, so a person in good times should not think he is safe (11:24), and one in bad times should not despair.

a: on the day a person dies
t: Judgment on the day of death
p: Ben Sira places God's final repayment at the day of death; the New Testament places a judgment after it.
b: The Greek en hēmera teleutēs means "on the day of the end, of death." For Ben Sira, God can settle accounts even at the last moment of life: a hard death can undo a happy life (11:27), and so no one should be called blessed until he dies (11:28). This is judgment within this life, the view of Proverbs. The New Testament goes beyond it: "it is in store for human beings to die once, and after this, judgment" (Hebrews 9:27), and "all of us must be shown openly before the judgment seat of Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:10). Later Christian readers, reading the Latin "in die obitus," heard the moment of death as the moment of judgment.
orig: ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τελευτῆς (en hēmera teleutēs)

a: Do not call anyone blessed until he has died
t: "Call no man happy until he is dead"
p: The Greek historian Herodotus tells of Solon giving the same advice to King Croesus.
b: In Herodotus' Histories (1.32.7), written about 430 BC, the Athenian lawgiver Solon tells the rich king Croesus of Lydia that a man is worthy to be called fortunate only if he ends his life well: "refrain from calling him fortunate before he dies; call him lucky" (A. D. Godley's translation). Croesus later lost his kingdom. The saying was famous across the Greek world, and Ben Sira, who lived under Greek rule, may have known it as a proverb. But the thought also follows from his own teaching (11:26-27), so borrowing cannot be proved. He adds a Jewish note: a man is known "by his children."

a: Do not bring just anyone into your home
p: The rabbis quote this line of Ben Sira, and MS A has half of it.
b: The Babylonian Talmud quotes Ben Sira: "Prevent the multitudes from inside your house, and do not bring everyone into your house" (Sanhedrin 100b, in the William Davidson translation on Sefaria; Yevamot 63b gives the same advice). MS A (4v:18) has the second half of this saying: "Do not bring every man into your house" (Parker and Abegg). In Sanhedrin 100b Rav Yosef first says the book should not be read, then says that its good passages, this one among them, may be taught even in public.

a: Like a decoy partridge in its cage
p: Hunters used a caged partridge to lure wild ones into the trap.
b: The Greek perdix thēreutēs en kartallō is "a hunting partridge in a basket," a tame bird whose calls drew wild partridges into the net. So the proud man's heart lures others to their fall, while he watches like a spy. Jeremiah also uses the partridge (Jeremiah 17:11). MS A (4v:20) has "As a bird is seized in a cage" (Parker and Abegg). Just before it (4v:19-20) MS A has a line close to Jeremiah 5:27, "As a cage is full of birds, / so their houses are full of fraud," but several of its letters are uncertain and its last word is lost. The Talmud quotes that line from Ben Sira as "As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit" (Yevamot 63b, William Davidson translation).
orig: πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς ἐν καρτάλλῳ (perdix thēreutēs en kartallō)

a: One spark of fire makes a whole bed of coals
p: James uses a similar picture of how a little fire spreads.
b: "See how little a flame it takes to set a huge forest alight!" (James 3:5). Ben Sira's spark is the small beginning of a sinner's scheme, which grows into bloodshed. MS A (4v:24-25) reads מנצוץ ירבה גחלת, "from a spark the coals grow many," and the Talmud quotes "like a spark that ignites a coal" among Ben Sira's sayings (Yevamot 63b).

a: Take a stranger into your home
p: Ben Sira's caution stands beside the Bible's strong call to hospitality.
b: The Greek allotrios is "someone who belongs to others," an outsider, not necessarily a foreigner. Ben Sira warns that such a person can turn a household upside down. The 66 books also prize hospitality to strangers: Abraham welcomed three visitors (Genesis 18:1-8), the Law commands love for the foreigner (Deuteronomy 10:19), and Hebrews says, "Do not forget to welcome strangers, for by this some people have had angels as guests without knowing it" (Hebrews 13:2). Ben Sira's advice is prudence about letting someone settle in your home (Greek enoikison, "make him live with you"), not a refusal of help; he commands generosity elsewhere (7:32; 29:1-13).
orig: ἐνοίκισον ἀλλότριον (enoikison allotrion)

a: know who you are doing it for
p: An early Christian handbook passes on a saying close to this one.
b: The Didache, an early Christian handbook, first says, "Give to every one that asks you, and ask it not back," warns those who take without need, then adds a saying introduced with "it has been said": "Let your alms sweat in your hands, until you know to whom you should give" (Didache 1:6, in the translation on New Advent). The Didache names no source, and whether its saying goes back to Ben Sira cannot be shown; both advise giving with care, so that help does good. Ben Sira's reason here is practical: a kindness done to the right person is remembered with thanks.

a: if not by him, then by the Most High
p: Proverbs says that kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD.
b: Proverbs says, "Showing kindness to a poor man is a loan made to the LORD, / and he will pay him back for what he did" (Proverbs 19:17). Jesus goes further: give to those who cannot repay, "You will be paid back at the resurrection of the righteous" (Luke 14:14). Ben Sira looks for repayment in this life, from the person helped or from God.
orig: ἀλλὰ παρὰ Ὑψίστου (alla para Hypsistou)

a: someone who does not give alms
p: The Hebrew here has tsedaqah, as in 7:10.
b: The Greek tō eleēmosynēn mē charizomenō is "the one who does not freely give alms." MS A (5r:2-3) has וגם צדקה לא עשה, "and also did not do tsedaqah," the word for charity seen at 7:10. In MS A the first line speaks of "the one who comforts the wicked" (Parker and Abegg), that is, supports him, which fits the advice that follows (12:4-7).
orig: τῷ ἐλεημοσύνην μὴ χαριζομένῳ (tō eleēmosynēn mē charizomenō)

a: do not come to the aid of the sinner
p: Ben Sira's rule seems to clash with Proverbs 25:21 and with Jesus' command to love enemies.
b: Ben Sira says to give to the godly and not to help the sinner (12:4-7). Proverbs says, "If someone who hates you is hungry, feed him bread" (Proverbs 25:21), and Paul quotes it (Romans 12:20). Jesus taught, "keep loving your enemies, doing good, and lending without hoping for anything back... since he himself is kind to people who are ungrateful and evil" (Luke 6:35). Thomas Aquinas met these verses (12:4-6 in the Latin numbering) as an objection and answered: "We ought not to help a sinner as such, that is by encouraging him to sin, but as man, that is by supporting his nature" (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 32, article 9, reply to objection 1, in the English on New Advent). The text itself does not soften the rule.

a: or he will use it to get the better of you
p: The Hebrew phrase for "bread" can also be read as "war."
b: The Greek says, "hold back his bread... so that he does not overpower you with it." MS A (5r:4) reads כלי לחם אל תתן לו. Written without vowels, the letters can be read kele lechem, "utensils of bread," or kele lacham, "weapons of war," as Parker and Abegg translate, since l-ch-m is also the root "to fight" (as in Psalm 35:1). Either way, the danger is that your gift arms an enemy. The first line of the verse has a doubtful word too; see the variant on "the ungodly."
orig: ἐμπόδισον τοὺς ἄρτους αὐτοῦ (empodison tous artous autou), "block his bread"

a: the Most High himself hates sinners
p: Ben Sira agrees with some Psalms; the Wisdom of Solomon says God hates nothing he made.
b: Psalm 5:5 says to God, "You hate everyone who does wrong," and Psalm 11:5 says his soul hates the one who loves violence. Ben Sira uses this as a reason not to fund the ungodly, and MS A has the same thought: "For God also hates evil people" (5r:4-5, Parker and Abegg). The Wisdom of Solomon says, "You love all that is, / and nothing you made disgusts you" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:24), and Jesus speaks of the Father who "is kind to people who are ungrateful and evil" (Luke 6:35). The longer Greek adds a line here, which the KJV has; see the variant.
r: Psalm 5:5; Psalm 11:5; Wisdom of Solomon 11:24; Luke 6:35; Romans 5:8

a: A friend is not recognized when times are good
p: Proverbs also says true friendship shows itself in trouble.
b: Proverbs says, "At every time a friend keeps loving, / and a brother is born for the hard days" (Proverbs 17:17), and that wealth adds many friends while the poor man is deserted (Proverbs 19:4). Ben Sira made the same point in 6:8-12. Here the Plain English Translation departs from Swete's base text: Codex Vaticanus has a verb meaning "be avenged" or "be punished," and the Plain English Translation follows "be known," with a corrector of Sinaiticus, MS A and the Latin. See the variant.

a: like bronze his wickedness gathers rust
p: The Greek and Hebrew say bronze; the KJV says iron.
b: The Greek chalkos is copper or bronze, and ioutai means "corrodes, tarnishes." MS A (5r:8) has כי כנחשת רועו יחליא, "for like bronze his evil corrodes." Bronze does not rust away like iron; its surface goes green and dull, and must be polished again and again, as the next verse says. The KJV's "for like as iron rusteth" changes the metal.
orig: ὡς γὰρ ὁ χαλκὸς ἰοῦται (hōs gar ho chalkos ioutai)

a: someone who polishes a mirror
p: Ancient mirrors were polished bronze, and tarnish had to be rubbed off.
b: Mirrors in Ben Sira's world were disks of polished bronze, never perfectly clear (1 Corinthians 13:12; James 1:23). Tarnish built up, and the owner had to keep rubbing it off. Ben Sira's picture: treat your enemy like such a mirror, keep "polishing," watching him, and you will find his corrosion is not past cleaning, or perhaps that it was never gone. The last line is hard to read in Greek; MS A (5r:10-11) has "be to him like one who reveals a secret," and ends, "and know the end of jealousy."
orig: ὡς ἐκμεμαχὼς ἔσοπτρον (hōs ekmemachōs esoptron), "like one who has wiped a mirror"

a: my words will sting you
p: The Greek verb is the one Acts uses for hearers cut to the heart.
b: The Greek katanygēsē means "you will be pierced, stung" with regret. It is the verb of Acts 2:37: "These words pierced their hearts" (Greek katenygēsan). Here the teacher speaks in his own voice: if you seat your enemy at your right hand, the place of honor and trust (Psalm 110:1), one day you will remember what I told you, and it will hurt.
orig: κατανυγήσῃ (katanygēsē)

a: a snake charmer
p: Ecclesiastes and the Psalms also speak of snake charmers.
b: Snake charming was an old art in Egypt and the Near East. "If the snake bites when no spell has been whispered, / there is no gain for the master of the tongue" (Ecclesiastes 10:11), and the psalmist speaks of a cobra "that will not listen to the voice of the charmers" (Psalm 58:5). Ben Sira's point: no one pities a man who plays with danger and gets hurt; so it is with the one who keeps close company with a sinner (12:14).
orig: ἐπαοιδὸν ὀφιόδηκτον (epaoidon ophiodēkton), "a snake-bitten charmer"

a: With his lips the enemy makes his words sweet
p: Proverbs and the Psalms describe the same smiling enemy.
b: Proverbs warns, "When he makes his voice sweet, do not trust him, / for seven abhorrent things are in his heart" (Proverbs 26:25). The psalmist says of a false friend, "Softer than oil were his words, / and they were swords out of their sheaths" (Psalm 55:21). Ben Sira adds the tears: the enemy weeps with you in public and waits for his chance.

a: he will trip you by the heel
p: The picture of the treacherous friend who strikes at the heel is in the Psalms and in John.
b: The Greek hyposchasei pternan sou means "he will trip (or cut) your heel." The psalmist mourns a friend "who ate my bread" and "has raised his heel high against me" (Psalm 41:9), and Jesus applies that verse to Judas: "The one who eats my bread has raised his heel against me" (John 13:18). Jacob, whose name sounds like "heel," was born gripping Esau's heel (Genesis 25:26). MS A (5r:20) has 'aqev, "heel," too.
orig: ὑποσχάσει πτέρναν σου (hyposchasei pternan sou)

a: He will shake his head and clap his hands
p: Gestures of mockery and glee over someone's ruin.
b: Shaking the head and clapping the hands were gestures of scorn over someone ruined: "Everyone going by on the road claps hands over you; they whistle and wag their heads at Daughter Jerusalem" (Lamentations 2:15); "they sneer with their lips and shake their heads" (Psalm 22:7). At the cross, "Those walking past kept reviling him. They shook their heads" (Matthew 27:39). The false friend, once you fall, shows what he really thinks.
